A custom core editor requires coordinated source, header, and CMake changes. Its new directory and files must be added to editor build scripts, while public declarations, space-type registration, context accessors, and persistent DNA definitions must be updated where the new type crosses module boundaries.

The affected set is broader than the editor implementation because [[Blender Custom Editor Registration]] depends on window-manager startup and [[Blender Custom Editor RNA Integration]] depends on generated data descriptions. Missing one build or declaration path can leave the editor uncompiled or unreachable.

A custom deployment target publishes an application to infrastructure such as IIS or another destination configured outside a provider-managed default. It gives the team control over the host while also returning responsibility for its operating system, runtime, networking, and maintenance.

The book contrasts such targets with Azure App Service, which manages much of that infrastructure. Target choice therefore determines both the deployment mechanism and who owns continuing operational work.

A custom editor's header-region initialization callback prepares the [[Blender Region Structure]] for standard header behavior. The tutorial delegates this work to the common editor API instead of reproducing layout and handler setup inside the new editor.

The callback is installed on the header's [[Blender Region Type Structure]] during [[Blender Custom Editor Registration]]. Its matching draw path can then create a [[Blender UI Block]], define buttons, and perform [[Blender Editor Button Operator Binding]].

A custom editor's main-region initialization callback prepares its two-dimensional view state for the current width and height. The tutorial uses the [[Blender UI View2D API]] to reinitialize the region with a customizable common-view mode.

This setup gives the subsequent draw callback a coherent [[Blender View2D Region Coordinates]] system. The callback is registered in the main [[Blender Region Type Structure]] and runs when the editor or region requires size-dependent initialization.

A custom game scripting language is designed specifically around the concepts and workflows of one engine or project. It can expose concise domain operations and restrict features that would complicate execution or authoring.

The benefit of a tailored surface comes with the cost of implementing and maintaining lexical analysis, syntax analysis, execution, tools, documentation, and debugging that a mature general-purpose language already provides.

A cut-and-stack time plot divides a long time axis into overlapping segments and places those segments in aligned rows. It preserves an aspect ratio selected through [[Banking to 45 Degrees]] without producing an extremely wide or shallow figure. Small overlaps help the reader continue a trajectory across row boundaries. The layout improves local slope perception, but the discontinuous horizontal arrangement makes very long-range timing comparisons less immediate.

A cutscene is a section of a game devoted primarily to showing noninteractive story material. It can use animation, dialogue, still images, or other presentation and often appears between playable sections as an intermission.

Cutscenes can provide context and rest from [[Game Resistance|resistance]], but they place playing and watching beside one another rather than fully integrating them. Requiring timed input inside a cutscene adds exertion without necessarily making its choices meaningful.

A cyber deception outcome occurs when an attacker causes users or systems to accept false information, identities, or states as genuine. The harm is not limited to secret theft or interrupted service; corrupted trust can redirect decisions while systems appear available.

Authentication, integrity verification, provenance evidence, and independent confirmation help resist this outcome. Framing deception explicitly extends [[Outcome-Based Cyber Defense]] beyond confidentiality and availability alone.

A cyber threat is a circumstance or actor capable of causing harm to an information system or the assets it supports. A threat represents potential danger; it becomes an attack when someone takes action to exploit an opportunity.

Keeping threats distinct from [[Cyber Vulnerability]] and [[Security Risk]] makes analysis clearer. A system may contain a weakness without an active adversary, while a threat may exist without a usable path into that system.

A cyber vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited to violate a system's security goals. It may arise from software, configuration, architecture, procedure, or human behavior rather than from code alone.

A vulnerability does not by itself determine harm. [[Cyber Risk Formula]] relates it to the relevant [[Cyber Threat]] and the impact of a successful event, helping defenders prioritize weaknesses instead of treating every flaw as equally urgent.

A cybersecurity risk assessment identifies valued assets, relevant [[Cyber Threat|threats]], exploitable [[Cyber Vulnerability|vulnerabilities]], existing controls, and the likely impact of harmful events. It turns a broad concern about security into a prioritized account of what could happen and why it matters.

The result supports decisions about treatment, acceptance, transfer, or avoidance of risk. Because systems and threats change, assessment is a continuing process rather than a one-time checklist.

A cyclic group consists of all integer powers, or integer multiples, of one element. It is written ⟨a⟩, where a is a generator.

Every cyclic group is abelian, and every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic.

A cyclic module is generated by one element m. The map R → Rm sending r to rm is surjective, with kernel Ann(m), so Rm is isomorphic to R/Ann(m).

This description connects elements to ideals. A prime p is an [[Associated Prime]] of M exactly when M contains a cyclic submodule isomorphic to R/p.

A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on one circle. Opposite interior angles are supplementary because each is an inscribed angle intercepting arcs that together complete the circle. Conversely, a quadrilateral with supplementary opposite angles can be inscribed in a circle.

A dangling node in PageRank is a page with incoming links but no outgoing links. Its row in the [[Hyperlink Matrix]] contains only zeros, so rank flows into the node without being redistributed.

Uncorrected dangling nodes drain the total rank during repeated multiplication. The [[Random Surfer Model]] treats a surfer at such a dead end as able to jump to any page, replacing the zero row with equal transition probabilities.

A data analyst converts organized data into summaries, comparisons, and explanations that answer defined questions. The work emphasizes correct measures, suitable visualizations, and interpretation within the problem domain.

In the book's capability progression, analysis builds on sound data preparation and precedes the broader pattern discovery associated with a [[Data Miner]].

A data annotation is metadata attached to a model member to express mapping or validation rules. In an Entity Framework Core entity, annotations can identify keys, required values, lengths, or other constraints that cannot be inferred sufficiently from naming conventions alone.

Annotations supplement [[Convention over Configuration]]. They keep simple rules close to the entity definition, while more complicated mapping remains available through explicit model configuration.

A data archive preserves information that is no longer used regularly but must be retained for historical, regulatory, or compliance reasons. Search and retrieval over long retention periods matter more than immediate operational restoration.

An archive differs from a backup, whose purpose is rapid recovery of changing day-to-day data. Backup retention is commonly measured in weeks or months, while archival retention can extend for years or decades.

A data cache keeps a reusable result closer to the application so repeated requests do not always query the database. In-memory caching can shorten a read path for data whose temporary reuse is acceptable.

Caching introduces a freshness decision. The application needs a key, an expiration policy, and a reasoned response to writes so that lower latency does not silently serve unsuitable old data.

A data cube is a multidimensional arrangement of measures indexed by analytic dimensions. It makes common summaries and cross-sections efficient to retrieve from a large body of organizational data.

Users can slice, dice, pivot, drill down, or roll up the cube to explore patterns at different resolutions. These operations guide questions and preparation but do not replace statistical or machine-learning validation.

A data mart is a subset of enterprise data restricted to a particular subject area. It uses a consistent model and makes a focused collection available for efficient analysis.

A mart can reduce the amount of data scanned for a specific mining problem, but its narrower scope may omit relationships visible in the wider warehouse. Its boundaries should follow the analytical question rather than departmental convenience alone.

A data miner searches prepared datasets for predictive or descriptive patterns using statistical and machine-learning methods. The role must distinguish stable structure from artifacts of a particular sample through independent validation.

The book positions data mining between conventional analysis and the broader synthesis expected of a [[Data Scientist]].

A data ownership right would give a person or organization property-like control over data, potentially including powers to exclude others, transfer access, or seek remedies against interference. The source finds no general, specific property right in data under the Swiss and European rules it examines.

The term is still useful in a broader sense because control can arise through contracts, confidentiality, intellectual-property rules, tort remedies, or technical access. Each mechanism supplies different powers and binds different parties.

A data protection impact assessment examines a proposed processing operation before or during deployment to identify effects on people, justify the purpose, and select safeguards. It treats privacy risk as a property of the complete system rather than of isolated fields.

For large-scale analytics, the assessment must include linkage, inference, opaque processing, secondary uses, and the possibility of group-level harm. It complements individual notice when affected people cannot foresee every later analytical use.

A data record is a group of related fields describing one entity for an application. An email record, for example, can contain its sender, delivery date, subject, and message body.

A [[Sorting Algorithm]] reorders whole records according to selected fields called a [[Sort Key]]. The remaining fields travel with the record, so sorting changes position without altering the information represented by each entity.

A data repository is a concrete service that implements a set of persistence operations for an application. Its methods translate meaningful requests, such as retrieving a question or saving an answer, into database commands.

The repository keeps data-access details out of controllers and can be registered through dependency injection. Its method boundaries also expose where asynchronous execution and transaction decisions belong.

A data science pipeline is the sequence through which data are captured, cleaned, combined, selected, restructured, modeled, interpreted, and used for action. Ethical choices occur at every stage, not only when a finished model produces a decision.

Collection determines who becomes visible. Cleaning and selection decide which records count as errors or relevant evidence. Modeling chooses a target and a representation, while interpretation connects a statistical pattern to a real-world judgment. Because responsibility is distributed across this sequence, documenting transformations and decisions supports [[AI Traceability]] and makes hidden assumptions easier to challenge.

The book's CRISP-DM account makes the sequence iterative. Business understanding, data understanding, preparation, modeling, evaluation, and deployment can send work back to an earlier decision when data quality, model behavior, or practical usefulness falls short. The pipeline ends in a decision process and its monitoring, not in a model file.

A data scientist combines statistical reasoning, machine learning, software practice, and domain understanding to turn data into decisions. The role extends beyond producing a model because the scientist must also test assumptions, explain uncertainty, and make the analysis repeatable.

The book presents the role as a progression from data handling and analysis toward discovering patterns and creating new knowledge.

A data service centralizes client operations that exchange data with a back-end API. Instead of letting several components call [[Angular HttpClient]] directly, it provides named methods for getting, creating, and updating application records.

The layer creates one place for URL construction, response typing, post-processing, error handling, and retries. Domain-specific services can extend a typed base service while components depend on their narrower interfaces.

A data subject is the person to whom [[Personal Data]] relates. The concept ties information-processing duties to an individual even when the dataset uses an indirect identifier rather than a name.

In large combined datasets, identifying the subject can be uncertain because records may be linked or reattributed later. Rights and safeguards therefore depend on realistic possibilities of identification, not only on the label attached to a field.

A data technician prepares the foundations of analysis by acquiring, storing, cleaning, and organizing data. Reliable technical handling matters because errors in formats, types, or provenance can invalidate every later model.

This role anchors the first stage in the book's progression from raw data through analysis and mining to data science.

A data transfer object is a class shaped specifically for data sent across an application boundary. It can include values required by the client while omitting entity properties that should not be serialized or exposed.

Using a DTO preserves [[Separation of Concerns]] between persistence and presentation. It also gives tests a named, typed result, whereas a quick projection to an anonymous type is less reusable outside the method that created it.

In a domain-centered application, request DTOs form the [[Public API Contract]] rather than becoming domain objects. They favor serialization-friendly primitive values and carry data across the transport boundary; the [[Application Layer]] converts them into an [[Application Command]] or domain-specific values before invoking behavior. This prevents HTTP and serializer requirements from leaking into the [[Domain Model]].

A data value externality occurs when an organization captures benefits from data while shifting some costs or risks to people who generated, supplied, or are represented by it. Privacy loss, unfair profiling, and weakened bargaining power may remain outside the firm's price calculation.

Recognizing the externality explains why possession alone may not justify unrestricted use. Liability, access rights, compensation, or governance duties can be considered alongside ownership.

A data warehouse is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-varying, and generally non-updatable collection designed to support management decisions and business intelligence. It consolidates data from otherwise separate operational sources.

A common, high-quality repository gives data mining a consistent view of organizational history. It does not remove the need to understand provenance, definitions, or changes in source systems.

The book adds that a warehouse can materially shorten individual data science projects because extraction, standardization, and integration have already been done for shared use. Its historic records also allow models to be rolled through earlier time periods and checked for changing accuracy. A central repository is helpful, not a prerequisite for data science.

A data-driven culture expects claims and organizational choices to be informed by accessible evidence. It combines technical capability with routines for asking questions, challenging assumptions, sharing results, and revising action.

Culture matters because an accurate analysis has little effect if it is isolated from authority and workflow. Evidence must be understandable, timely, and connected to the people who can act on it.

A data-driven UI add-on combines script behavior with declarative data files so users or content authors can extend a game's interface without changing the engine. The files describe layout and metadata, while scripts respond to events and update elements.

Powerful extension points require a security boundary. Privileged operations can remain in protected engine code, with add-ons permitted to observe or hook approved behavior rather than replace core functions.

A database context is the Entity Framework Core object that represents a session with the database and coordinates entity sets, mappings, queries, and saved changes. An application-specific context declares the entities that belong to its model.

The context is configured with a database provider and connection information, then supplied to controllers or services through [[Dependency Injection]]. Tests can replace the production configuration with an [[In-Memory Database Provider]].

A database migration is an ordered, repeatable change that advances a database schema or required data from one version to the next. Applied migrations are journaled so the same change is not executed again on a later startup.

Migration scripts allow the database and application to evolve together. They should be additive and reviewable enough that deployment can determine what will change before the new application depends on it.

A database round trip is one request-response exchange between the application and its database. Each trip includes more than query execution: a connection path, command transfer, result transfer, and application-side processing all contribute latency.

Repeated queries inside a loop can make round trips grow with the number of parent records. Combining related work through joins or multiple result sets can reduce that cost when the resulting query and mapping remain manageable.

A database transaction groups operations so they either succeed as a unit or are rolled back together. EF Core applies transactional behavior when saving a compatible group of changes and also permits explicit transaction control for broader workflows.

Transactions protect consistency, but long-running transactions hold resources and can increase contention. A transaction boundary should therefore contain the smallest coherent business operation and define how failures are surfaced or retried.

A database-backed CMS import maps existing records into the content types, identifiers, and relationships expected by the new system. It must preserve meaning while translating source fields into structured pages, posts, components, or media references.

Reliable imports are repeatable, validated, and explicit about conflicts and missing data. Running them as a controlled migration is safer than embedding one-time assumptions in ordinary request handling.

A dataflow architecture expresses computation as components connected by the movement of data. A source produces measurements, filters transform them, and consumers use the resulting values for simulation, interaction, or rendering.

The structure suits AR pipelines because components can be developed and tested separately, then connected locally or across hosts. Scheduling and buffering must preserve acceptable latency and ensure that data dependencies update coherently.

A dataflow graph represents processing components as nodes and their data dependencies as directed connections. A change from a tracker can propagate through transformation, filtering, interaction, and rendering nodes toward a displayed result.

The graph makes the pipeline inspectable and reconfigurable. Cycles, differing update rates, threads, and distributed connections require an execution policy that prevents uncontrolled latency or inconsistent values.

In large-scale data processing, a compiler can translate a high-level script into successive logical and physical dataflow graphs. Operators form the nodes, directed dependencies determine execution order, and optimization rewrites the graph before distributed jobs are generated.

A DataFrame is a distributed collection organized into named columns with known structure. The schema gives a query optimizer more semantic information than an opaque collection of application objects.

In Spark SQL, DataFrame operations and relational queries can share an optimized execution plan while remaining connected to the broader Spark runtime.

A dataset dimension review checks the number of rows and columns immediately after import. Comparing the observed dimensions with an expected count can expose a wrong delimiter, dropped records, duplicated headers, or an unintended file.

Dimension review is a quick first step before examining classes, names, distributions, and missingness.

A dataset glimpse is a compact inspection of a table's dimensions, column names, variable types, and sample values. It helps an analyst spot obvious schema problems without printing the entire dataset.

The book uses this review early in ingestion so character, factor, date, and numeric fields can be corrected before modeling.

A dataset may also contain several defensible organizations. [[Alternative and Ensemble Clustering]] either seeks a substantially different view from an existing solution or combines many candidate partitions into a consensus. Alternative clustering can use explicit constraints, orthogonality, or information-theoretic objectives to avoid rediscovering the same structure. Ensemble methods work from co-association, voting, probabilistic combination, or consensus optimization. Diversity among inputs is valuable only when the component solutions retain useful signal; otherwise an ensemble can merely stabilize shared error.

[[C++ Clustering Software Design]] connects these mathematical families to reusable implementation. It models datasets, distances, clusters, arguments, algorithm lifecycles, and results as cooperating C++ abstractions, then uses design patterns to keep shared control flow separate from method-specific computation. Its implementations of hierarchical, partitional, fuzzy, model-based, genetic, subspace, and parallel algorithms show how software architecture can make experiments consistent without erasing the distinctive mathematics of each method.

Finally, [[Cluster Validity and Simulation]] determines whether the output deserves interpretation. External measures compare clusters with known labels, internal measures balance cohesion and separation, and relative measures compare algorithms or parameter choices. Pair-counting, information-theoretic, silhouette, stability, and Monte Carlo procedures illuminate different failure modes. No single score can certify that a clustering is true. Validation must connect the algorithm's assumptions, the chosen representation, perturbation behavior, and the application purpose. Together, these topics form a disciplined workflow: select informative structure, choose an algorithm whose biases fit it, preserve uncertainty and scale where necessary, and test whether the discovered organization remains useful under credible alternatives.

A dataset structure check verifies the shape and schema of data immediately after import. It compares observed row and column counts, names, classes, storage modes, levels, and missingness with the expected metadata.

This check catches silent transformations such as renamed variables, unexpected factor conversion, or a source field read with the wrong type. Later statistical output cannot repair a mismatch introduced at import, so structural validation belongs at the beginning of the pipeline.

The book operationalizes structure review through dimensions, a compact glimpse, first and last records, and random rows. These complementary views expose both schema-wide problems and malformed observations that a single preview might miss.

A date difference is the elapsed time between two parsed dates, often expressed in days. It can measure follow-up from an index event to a reference date or help determine whether a later event falls inside a predefined observation window.

The operation is meaningful only after both operands have valid date classes and a clear temporal interpretation. A fixed calendar censoring date and a subject-specific window, such as sixty days after discharge, answer different questions.

A datum is a recorded representation of some aspect of the world, not the aspect itself. A row may stand for a customer, transaction, or event, but the selected fields capture only the properties that collection systems could observe and that analysts chose to retain.

This distinction matters when interpreting results. A model learns relationships among recorded attributes; omitted circumstances and measurement choices remain outside its view. Treating the dataset as a partial abstraction encourages domain checks before a statistical pattern is converted into a claim about people or causes.

A DBSCAN border point has fewer than MinPts observations in its own Eps neighborhood but lies within the neighborhood of a core point. It belongs to a cluster without being able to initiate further dense expansion.

Its assignment can depend on which adjacent cluster reaches it first when dense regions are close.

A DBSCAN core point has at least MinPts observations inside its Eps neighborhood. It represents a locally dense location from which the algorithm can expand a cluster.

Core points connected through chains of dense neighborhoods belong to the same cluster. Nearby non-core observations may be included as border points.

A DBSCAN noise point is neither a core point nor a border point under the selected Eps and MinPts parameters. It is left outside the discovered density-connected clusters.

Noise is a model-relative label, not proof of error. Changing the radius, minimum count, metric, or data representation can change the classification.

A DCT coefficient histogram counts how often a selected discrete-cosine-transform coefficient takes each value across JPEG blocks. Ordinary single compression usually produces a comparatively smooth distribution centered around zero, with shape varying by spatial frequency and image content.

Periodic holes and peaks can expose [[Double Quantization Artifact]]. Analysts examine several frequencies because not every coefficient carries a clear trace, and heavy recompression or limited image area can weaken the statistical evidence.

A dead-end reward acknowledges or entices the player without feeding back into the main game system. A noninteractive story segment or platform-level [[Achievement]] may be rewarding while leaving the player's available verbs, resources, and choices unchanged.

These rewards can still provide rest, meaning, or motivation, but they risk eclipsing the pleasure of play when the player treats gameplay only as a barrier to the next payoff.

A deadlock arises when participants wait permanently for resources held by one another. A classic case occurs when two threads acquire the same pair of locks in opposite orders and each waits for the lock held by the other.

Consistent lock ordering, smaller critical sections, time-bounded acquisition, and fewer shared resources reduce the risk. Asynchronous code should also avoid synchronously blocking on incomplete tasks, which can create a waiting cycle with a captured execution context.

A debugger runs a program under controlled conditions so a developer can inspect its behavior and changing state. It can pause execution, step through instructions, and display variables, the call stack, and other runtime information.

In a full-stack application, [[Server-Side Debugging]] follows .NET request handling while [[Client-Side Debugging]] follows TypeScript and browser behavior. Both use breakpoints to stop at relevant operations.

A decider is a logical branch that routes a flow according to internal state, available resources, or external conditions. It represents a decision point inside a system model.

The conditions governing a decider should remain near the same organizational level and operational context as the decision. Excessive dependence across distant levels makes a [[System]] harder to understand and more brittle.

A decision boundary separates the regions of input space that a [[Classifier]] assigns to different outcomes. In two dimensions it can be visualized as a line or curve between classes.

A single [[Perceptron]] can learn only a linear boundary, so it handles data that can be divided by one straight line. An [[Artificial Neural Network]] with hidden layers can combine neuron outputs to represent more complicated, nonlinear boundaries.

Kelleher's two-input threshold-neuron example makes the geometry concrete. The boundary is perpendicular to the neuron's input-weight vector; altering the weights rotates it, while a [[Neural Network Bias|bias term]] moves it off the origin. That separates the effects of weight direction and threshold position on which [[Model Input Space|input points]] receive high activation.

A decision rule path is the conjunction of attribute-value tests encountered from a decision tree's root to one leaf. The leaf label supplies the consequence of the corresponding if-then rule.

Extracting one rule per path turns a tree into an explicit rule set. Pruning can remove conditions that mainly reflect noise.

A decision tree represents classification as a hierarchy of attribute tests. Internal nodes test features, branches correspond to outcomes, and leaf nodes return class labels.

Every root-to-leaf path can be read as an if-then rule. Tree depth and branching affect storage, search cost, and interpretability.

The book fits a classification tree as an interpretable baseline, examines its splits and variable importance, and applies it to held-out data. The contrast between training and validation results shows why readable structure does not eliminate the need for independent evaluation.

A decision variable represents a quantity whose value the optimization process is allowed to choose. Examples include production amounts, resource allocations, or activity levels.

Its coefficients in the [[Linear Objective Function]] measure value or cost, while its coefficients in each [[Linear Constraint]] measure resource use or other effects.

A decision-making design value specifies where players should choose, which consequences should matter, and how much information should be available at the moment of choice. It identifies the intended relationship between deliberation and action.

This value can call for transparent optimization, bluffing under hidden information, rapid commitment, or reflective ambiguity. The interface and feedback should preserve that intended decision condition rather than accidentally resolving or obscuring it.

A decision-oriented design meeting has a defined purpose, prepared questions, appropriate participants, and an explicit record of conclusions and actions. It uses synchronous time for issues that need interaction rather than for reporting information that could be shared asynchronously.

Closing the meeting requires identifying what was decided, what remains open, who will act, and when the result will be reviewed. Without that conversion, discussion creates motion but not progress.

A decorator implements the same interface as an object it wraps, delegates the core operation to that object, and adds behavior around it. The book's message decorators change console color while leaving simple or alert message classes responsible for their own output. Wrapping can be composed or selected at runtime, extending behavior without requiring a subclass for every combination of features.

A deep belief network stacks latent layers so that higher levels capture progressively abstract structure. It can be initialized by training restricted Boltzmann machines one layer at a time and then refined for a generative or supervised task.

Layer-wise learning historically made deep representation training more feasible. The final hidden activations can serve as derived features even when the network is later paired with a separate predictor.

A deep Boltzmann machine is an undirected graphical model with multiple layers of hidden variables. Interactions across layers let it represent complex dependencies and learn hierarchical latent features.

Unlike a directed stack, inference involves jointly explaining observations through the hidden layers. This expressiveness makes both inference and training computationally demanding and dependent on approximation.

A deep neural network is an [[Artificial Neural Network]] with multiple learned layers between input and output. Successive layers can transform raw features into progressively more useful internal representations.

Depth lets a system learn complex mappings used in speech and language, but it also increases demands for data, computation, and careful optimization through [[Backpropagation]].

Each [[Hidden Layer]] encodes a transformation of the representation produced before it. Successive layers can therefore build a hierarchy of concepts: an image network might progress from local edges to parts and then complete objects. This increasing level of abstraction is the sense in which the network and its learning are described as deep.

Kelleher counts [[Neural Depth Counting|depth]] by learned transformations: the hidden layers plus the output layer, or the number of weight matrices crossed. The input layer merely presents values. Additional depth increases representational flexibility, but it can also aggravate the [[Vanishing Gradient Problem]] unless the architecture and training setup support useful backward signals.

A default prop supplies a component input when the consumer does not provide its optional value. It lets the common behavior remain concise while allowing a caller to override it explicitly.

For a function component, a value can be defaulted while destructuring the props parameter. The TypeScript prop remains optional to callers even though rendering receives a usable value.

A Definition of Done is the shared quality threshold every completed increment must satisfy. It can cover integration, testing, asset validation, performance, platform behavior, and any other conditions needed for stakeholders to inspect the result honestly.

The standard is negotiated and strengthened as the product matures. It makes remaining debt visible but does not claim that every increment is ready for final commercial deployment.

A definition of life commonly combines autonomous metabolism and growth, response to environmental stimuli, and reproduction. No single definition is universally accepted, especially for systems that possess only some of these properties.

Biofabricated tissues metabolize, grow, and respond, yet usually depend on external support and cannot reproduce the complete engineered object, placing them near a conceptual boundary.

A degree shift M(d) reindexes a [[Graded Module]] by defining its degree-t component to be M_{d+t}. The underlying module does not change; only the recorded degrees move.

Shifted copies of a ring are the building blocks of a [[Graded Free Module]]. Their shifts record the degrees of generators and appear in graded Betti numbers and Hilbert-series calculations.

A dendrogram is a tree diagram for a hierarchical clustering. Each node represents a cluster, connecting lines show which groups are nested, and the vertical level records when a merge or split occurs.

A horizontal cut through the dendrogram selects one partition from the hierarchy. The diagram makes the sequence visible, but the chosen cut still requires a stopping rule and substantive interpretation.

In the source's tissue example, leaf colors reveal whether an unsupervised hierarchy corresponds to known biological groups. Changes caused by feature scaling or by replacing all genes with leading principal components demonstrate that the tree depends on the representation and distance used.

Murtagh treats a ranked dendrogram as an ultrametric representation: the level of the first common ancestor gives a tree-derived distance between two leaves. Reversing the left and right children at a node changes the drawing order but preserves nested membership. A root-to-leaf path can also carry signed details in a hierarchical Haar transform, turning the tree into a multiscale data encoding.

A denoising autoencoder receives a corrupted version of an input but is trained to reconstruct the clean original. Successful reconstruction requires learning stable structure rather than simply copying individual values.

The corruption process defines which variations the representation should ignore. Features learned this way can be more robust and can initialize deeper models or support downstream tasks.

A dense layer is a [[Neural Network Layer]] in which every neuron receives connections from every unit in the preceding layer. Each connection has its own [[Neural Network Weight]], and each receiving neuron has a bias.

Dense connectivity is simple and flexible but creates many parameters. A layer of 128 neurons following 784 input values requires 100,352 separate connection weights, illustrating how network size can grow even with only a few layers.

A dense layer near the end of a [[Convolutional Neural Network]] can connect each of its neurons to all outputs from earlier filters. Unlike the shared weights within a convolutional filter, each dense neuron learns its own weights for combining those inputs.

This stage lets different neurons integrate the [[CNN Filter Bank|filter bank's]] local detections in different ways, such as relating simpler visual patterns to a whole-object decision. It is not another convolution: the dense connections collect information across the filter outputs rather than repeatedly applying one kernel to neighboring patches.

A density-based outlier lies in a region substantially sparser than the relevant surrounding data. It is judged relative to local concentration rather than one global distance threshold.

This perspective handles variable-density data better than a simple radius rule, but estimating neighborhood density and selecting its scale can be computationally demanding.

A dependency graph records which values or objects must be updated when another value changes. Unlike a scene graph's spatial hierarchy, its edges express computation: a tracked pose may affect a transformation, which affects a camera, which affects a rendered image.

Combining dependency and scene relationships lets an AR framework update derived state without hard-coding one procedural sequence. The scheduler still must handle cycles and timing constraints deliberately.

A dependency-injection implementation factory is a registration callback that constructs the service supplied for a contract. It is useful when construction needs configuration or when several interfaces must resolve to the same underlying object. The book registers read and write inventory interfaces through factory functions returning one context instance, preserving shared state while keeping each consumer dependent on only the operations it needs.

A deployment environment is a named operating context with its own configuration, infrastructure, diagnostics, and security expectations. Development, staging, and production environments let the same application select settings appropriate to different parts of delivery.

ASP.NET Core can load environment-specific configuration files and behavior. The environment name should be set by the host rather than embedded into the application source.

A deployment stage applies a selected build artifact and environment configuration to a target. Stages let a release pipeline model destinations such as staging and production as ordered steps with separate variables and conditions.

The stage should deploy an existing artifact rather than silently compile a new one. This preserves the evidence gathered earlier in the pipeline as the release advances.

A depth cue is information the visual system uses to infer the spatial structure and distance of objects. Depth cues support [[Object Selection]], [[3D Manipulation]], and [[Navigation]].

Static monocular cues include relative size, height relative to the horizon, occlusion, linear and aerial perspective, shadows, lighting, and texture gradients. Motion can provide parallax. The eyes also supply cues through [[Accommodation]], [[Vergence]], and binocular disparity.

Cues can reinforce or contradict one another. A display that presents inconsistent depth information can cause false spatial judgments, discomfort, or reduced performance, so cue support is an important part of [[Display Fidelity]].

A depth map can displace a copy of a single image sideways to synthesize another eye view. The two views then differ in image-space position according to estimated depth, giving a limited stereo effect. The book notes that this simple method can work in some shots but that displacing actual 3D geometry may yield a more natural result. The map itself is still an interpretation made from roto, procedural extraction, a depth sensor, or their combination. See [[Roto-Gradient Depth Maps for Stereo]] and [[Rubber-Sheet Stereo Conversion]].

A derivation is a sequence of [[Production Rule|production-rule]] applications that begins with a grammar's start symbol and produces another string. A terminal-only result belongs to the language generated by the grammar.

A left derivation always replaces the leftmost nonterminal, while a right derivation always replaces the rightmost. Restricting the order removes irrelevant differences and makes ambiguity and parsing procedures easier to analyze through a [[Parse Tree]].

A derivative describes the rate at which a function changes at a particular point. Geometrically, it is the slope of the tangent line at that point.

Its sign provides local directional information. If increasing a parameter produces a negative derivative of loss, the loss decreases; if the derivative is positive, increasing that parameter raises the loss. A multivariable function has a [[Partial Derivative]] for each variable.

Formally, the derivative is the limit of the difference quotient $(f(x+h)-f(x))/h$ as $h$ approaches zero, when that limit exists. Higher derivatives describe changes in earlier derivatives, and the second derivative supplies curvature information for identifying local extrema.

A derived class extends a [[Base Class]] and inherits its accessible members. It can add specialized behavior or override inherited behavior while preserving a shared abstraction.

City and country form components can derive from one base form component, and their services can derive from a generic data-service base. This removes repetition without forcing unrelated details into the parent.

A derived SI unit is an algebraic combination of [[SI Base Unit]]s. Force, for example, has base units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$ and is named the newton; energy has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$ and is named the joule. Expressing a named unit in base units makes dimensional consistency visible.

A derived SI unit is built by multiplying or dividing base units. The book's Table 2-2 writes force as the newton, $\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$, and pressure as the pascal, $\mathrm{Pa}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$. Special names make frequently used combinations shorter without changing their dimensional structure. Radian and steradian are listed with a unit expression of one because matching lengths or areas cancel. See [[Seven SI Base Units]] and [[Dimensional Homogeneity in Equations]].

A derived temporal feature converts a date or time into an analytically useful component such as year, month, weekday, or season. The transformation can expose periodic or long-term structure that a raw timestamp does not express directly.

Derivation rules must match the relevant calendar, timezone, and domain definitions.

A descendant combinator matches an element anywhere inside another matched element, regardless of the number of intervening generations. It is represented by whitespace between selectors.

A child combinator, written with `>`, requires the second subject to be an immediate child of the first. The distinction lets selectors use document structure either broadly or narrowly without altering the markup.

A design discussion queue records questions and disagreements that need collective judgment but are not yet actionable tasks. Keeping them separate prevents unresolved decisions from being disguised as assignments.

Each entry should name the issue, the evidence or constraint behind it, and when a decision becomes necessary. The team can then use meeting time on choices that actually block progress.

A design matrix places one experimental unit in each row and one modeled term in each column. Its entries encode the intercept, group indicators, continuous predictors, transformations, and interactions used to explain the outcome vector.

The matrix is both a mathematical and scientific specification. Choosing its columns determines which coefficients can be estimated and what each one means; R's `model.matrix` exposes the representation generated from a model formula.

A design pattern becomes concrete only after each abstract participant is mapped to a class and responsibility in the application. For a clustering Composite, Node is the component, LeafNode is the leaf, and InternalNode is the composite that owns children.

Writing the mapping prevents pattern names from replacing design reasoning. It clarifies which object controls creation, which interface clients use, and which dependency is intended to vary.

A design pattern is useful when it names a recurring problem, identifies the forces that make the problem difficult, and offers a reusable arrangement of responsibilities. It is not a command to add classes or infrastructure wherever the pattern can be recognized. [[Software Design Principles]] provides the criteria for deciding whether a proposed structure helps. DRY asks whether one fact or behavior has been duplicated; KISS asks whether accidental complexity can be removed; YAGNI asks whether speculative features are being built before they are needed. A minimum viable product limits a delivery to the smallest useful set of behavior, while the SOLID principles ask how reasons for change, extensibility, substitutability, interface size, and dependency direction affect maintainability. These principles complement one another: abstraction can remove harmful duplication, but an abstraction introduced too early can violate simplicity and create work for a requirement that never arrives.

[[Object-Oriented Design Patterns]] translates those concerns into collaborations among objects. Creational patterns separate the decision to construct an object from the code that uses it. An abstract factory chooses a related family of products; a factory method delegates selection to a creator; a builder organizes a complex construction process; a prototype copies an existing object; and a singleton constrains instance count. Structural and behavioral patterns change how objects interact. A decorator wraps one object to add behavior without rewriting the wrapped implementation. A chain of responsibility passes a request among handlers, an observer publishes state changes to subscribers, a strategy selects one algorithm from several, and a command represents a request as an object. Their value lies in the particular seam they create for change, not in the number of pattern names an application contains.

The application must still create and connect its concrete objects. [[.NET Dependency Injection and Service Lifetimes]] moves that work to a composition boundary. Dependency inversion says high-level behavior should depend on stable abstractions rather than construction details; dependency injection is one way to supply the concrete implementations. The .NET service collection records mappings and lifetimes, and the service provider resolves them when needed. Transient instances are created on demand, scoped instances are shared within a defined boundary such as a web request, and singleton instances are shared across a provider. An implementation factory handles construction that needs explicit logic. These lifetimes do not make mutable code safe: a singleton used from several requests can still suffer races, and building a second service provider does not preserve the first provider's singleton identity.

A design revision decision chooses which evaluated response will enter the next prototype. It weighs fit with design values, expected effect, cost, risk, dependencies, and what the revision will make possible to learn.

The decision should also record what is deliberately not being changed. This protects a focused test from accumulating unrelated improvements that obscure whether the chosen response worked.

A design should state the intended balance among practiced skill, forward-looking strategy, randomized events, and uncertainty from hidden or interacting causes. Each produces a different basis for success and a different emotional rhythm.

Making the balance explicit prevents one source from erasing the others. Excessive randomness can make developed skill irrelevant, while complete predictability can eliminate the uncertainty that gives strategic commitment its tension.

A deterministic context-free language L is one for which a deterministic [[Pushdown Automaton]] accepts the strings of L followed by a distinct end marker. The marker lets the machine distinguish an actual end of input from a point where more symbols might still arrive.

Nondeterminism adds genuine recognition power to pushdown automata, so some context-free languages are not deterministic context-free. Deterministic context-free languages support efficient parsing methods such as [[LL(1) Parsing]] and [[LR(1) Parsing]].

A deterministic finite-state automaton is a five-part machine (Q, Σ, q₀, δ, F): a finite state set, input alphabet, start state, total transition function, and set of accepting states. Every state-symbol pair selects exactly one next state.

The machine accepts a [[String]] when consuming the entire string from q₀ ends in F. Its states summarize only the finite information about the processed prefix that is relevant to future acceptance.

A development environment is configured for creating and diagnosing an application. It may enable detailed error pages, verbose logging, development signing material, and tooling that should not be exposed publicly.

Environment-specific configuration can override general settings without changing production values. Publishing an application must explicitly select the intended [[Production Environment]] rather than carrying development diagnostics forward.

A Development Team is the group that selects how to turn backlog items into a completed [[Product Increment]]. It plans and monitors its own work, adapts daily, and demonstrates the result rather than receiving a detailed task plan from a manager.

A game Development Team needs the disciplines required to deliver integrated, playable value. Shared accountability applies to the increment even when individual members retain specialties.

A diagonal matrix is a [[Square Matrix]] whose off-diagonal entries are all zero. Its main diagonal can contain arbitrary values.

Diagonal matrices are inexpensive to multiply, invert when every diagonal entry is nonzero, and raise to powers. [[Matrix Diagonalization]] seeks a representation in which a matrix becomes diagonal because computations then reduce to independent scalar operations.

A dial-up modem translated computer data into audio tones that could travel over ordinary telephone lines and converted received tones back into bits. Users called a local service number from a personal computer.

The connection reused widespread voice infrastructure but was slow and often billed by time or distance. It gave households access to databases, bulletin boards, and online services before broadband.

A dialog manager chooses what an assistant should do next after receiving an interpreted user input. It combines the current [[Meaning Representation]] with conversation state, personal or display context, external results, and a [[Dialog Policy]].

Its actions can include asking for missing information, clarifying ambiguity, invoking a service, presenting a result, or recovering from an error. It therefore coordinates the other modules of the [[Virtual Assistant Pipeline]].

A dialog module is a reusable subflow for a recurring conversational function such as confirmation, help, authentication, or collecting an address. It packages related states and transitions behind a defined entry and exit.

Modules reduce duplication in a [[Finite-State Dialog Manager]] and make common recovery behavior consistent. They also expose clearer boundaries for testing and maintenance.

A dialog policy maps the current conversational state to the assistant's next action. The policy encodes choices such as whether to ask, confirm, execute, wait, or recover.

A policy can be hand-authored as a [[Finite-State Dialog Manager]] or learned through [[Reinforcement Learning]]. In either case, it must balance task completion, efficiency, error risk, and the user's interaction expectations.

A dialog transition moves a finite-state interaction from one state to another after an event. Events can include a recognized user value, a no-match condition, timeout, help request, service result, or error.

Transitions make recovery behavior explicit in a [[Finite-State Dialog Manager]]. Their number can grow rapidly when every exceptional path is copied across many states.

A dialog turn is one participant's contribution before control passes to the other participant. In a voice interface, turn boundaries are inferred from speaking, silence, prompts, and interruption rather than explicit message submission.

The [[Dialog Manager]] uses turn state to decide when to listen, respond, wait, or accept an [[Interjection]]. Poor turn handling can make an accurate assistant feel slow or unresponsive.

A dialogue tree documents a scripted conversation as player choices and corresponding non-player-character responses. Each exchange can lead to another set of options, end the conversation, or trigger a game or story consequence.

The tree makes authored possibilities tractable without requiring unrestricted natural-language understanding. Designers must control branching growth and write options that accurately signal the avatar's intended meaning.

A diesel-engine plant burns fuel and converts hot gas energy into piston motion inside its engine cylinders. The engine rotates a generator to make electricity. The source places this arrangement in local backup service and lower-demand areas away from long grid lines. Exhaust and cooling-jacket heat can also be recovered in a [[Cogeneration Power Plant]].

A differential analyzer is an analog computer that solves differential equations by linking mechanical integrators. Vannevar Bush developed influential versions at MIT that represented mathematical relationships through rotating disks and shafts.

The machine supported scientific calculation and wartime firing tables. Its physical modeling approach also shaped proposals for electronic computers, even as digital numerical methods ultimately became dominant.

A differential backup copies files that changed since the most recent [[Full Backup]]. Each later differential grows to include every change accumulated after that common full snapshot.

Restoring the complete fileset generally requires the last full backup and the latest differential. This uses less storage than repeated full backups and fewer sets than a long incremental chain, while making individual-file location more complex than a single full set.

A difficulty mode is a player-selected configuration that changes how much resistance a game presents. It can alter rules, resources, timing, enemy behavior, or other demands to create different pacing through the same underlying system.

Choosing a mode before play creates a paradox: the player may not yet understand the game well enough to know which setting will be satisfying. Multiple modes can also imply that one is the intended experience, so their effects should be made understandable and revisable where possible.

A diffraction grating contains many equally spaced parallel slits. Their diffracted waves interfere to form narrow principal maxima satisfying $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$, where $d$ is slit spacing. More illuminated slits sharpen the maxima, allowing wavelength measurement and separation of spectral components with greater resolving power.

A digital elevation model stores sampled elevation in a grid whose values can drive displacement of a subdivided plane. A dark-looking DEM may hold useful values in a narrow range, so levels can reveal its heights before it is applied. Subdivision must be increased cautiously: too little looks jagged, while excessive detail burdens the machine. The book notes that radar-derived elevation may represent the first reflected surface, including treetops or buildings, rather than bare ground. A matching aerial image can texture the resulting terrain. See [[Manual Perspective-Plane Scene Extraction]] for another source-image-to-scene method.

A digital footprint is the collection of traces associated with a person's activities across physical and online systems. The book distinguishes data knowingly made public from a data shadow: records gathered about a person without their knowledge, consent, or awareness.

Even deliberate sharing offers limited control once records are combined or repurposed. Likes, purchases, locations, and call metadata can support inferences about traits never disclosed explicitly. Privacy analysis must therefore consider what a dataset enables others to infer, not only what the original field appears to reveal.

A digital input device reports discrete states, commonly interpreted as on or off. Keyboard keys and gamepad buttons are examples, but useful game behavior usually requires more meaning than the current binary value.

Comparing present and previous states yields transitions such as just pressed and just released. Those transitions distinguish a single command from an action intended to continue while the control is held.

A digital signature uses a private key to sign data and a corresponding public key to verify the result. Verification provides evidence that the signed content has not changed and that the signer possessed the private key.

Practical signature APIs usually hash the message and apply an asymmetric algorithm such as RSA to the digest using a defined padding scheme. Trust in the signature still depends on securely associating the public key with the claimed identity.

Digital signatures support [[Nonrepudiation]] by giving a recipient verifiable evidence that the holder of a private key signed particular content. The public key checks that evidence, while a certificate or other trusted association is still needed to connect the key to a claimed sender.

A direct game action changes an object or playspace through the player's immediate operation, such as moving a piece or aiming an avatar. An indirect action produces effects through a mediated system, delayed consequence, delegated unit, or chain of rules.

The distinction concerns causal distance, not importance. Indirect actions can create strategy by requiring the player to predict how a present decision will propagate through the [[Game State Snapshot|game state]].

A direct manipulation interface lets users act on visible objects through pointing, dragging, and selection while receiving immediate feedback. The actions resemble operations on physical objects more than memorized command syntax.

Graphical displays and the mouse made this interaction practical. Its effectiveness depends on clear visual representations and predictable relationships between gestures and system state.

A direct methanol fuel cell feeds liquid methanol to an electrode without first reforming it into a separate hydrogen supply. Its polymer electrolyte passes protons, and the net reaction with oxygen produces water and carbon dioxide. This fuel-handling distinction makes it different from a [[Hydrogen-Oxygen Fuel Cell]], even though both produce current by transporting ions internally and electrons through a load.

A direct proof of p → q assumes p and uses definitions, established results, and valid deductions to obtain q. For a universally quantified claim, the argument begins with an arbitrary member of the domain so that the conclusion applies to every member rather than a special case.

Direct proofs often succeed by translating abstract properties into their defining equations and then transforming those equations until the desired property becomes visible.

A directed acyclic graph is a [[Directed Graph]] containing no [[Graph Cycle]]. It is commonly abbreviated DAG.

DAGs represent relationships that proceed in one direction without eventually returning to their starting point. Task priorities, prerequisites, and dependencies fit this structure when following the directed relationships can never lead back to an earlier item.

A directed graph is a [[Graph]] whose edges have directions. An edge from vertex $A$ to vertex $B$ does not imply that another edge leads back from $B$ to $A$.

The web is directed because one page may link to another without receiving a return link. Directed graphs can contain cycles, while a [[Directed Acyclic Graph]] prohibits them and is useful for dependency and prerequisite relationships.

A directed minimum spanning tree restricts a learned Bayesian network to a tree-shaped dependency structure. Pairwise relationship weights identify a connecting tree, which is then oriented to obtain a directed probabilistic decomposition.

The restriction makes structure identification tractable and exposes important dependencies, but it cannot represent every pattern of interaction. Its simplicity is both the computational advantage and the modeling limitation.

A directed prompt asks a focused question whose likely answers belong to a known set or semantic type. It communicates what information is needed and constrains the next recognition and understanding task.

Directed prompts can improve recovery by offering alternatives or examples. Overuse, however, turns a flexible assistant into a rigid [[Directed Dialog]] that prevents users from volunteering useful information.

A directional derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change of a multivariable function in a chosen unit direction $u$. For a differentiable function, it is $D_u f(x)=\nabla f(x)\cdot u$.

The [[Gradient]] supplies all such first-order directional information. Its direction gives the steepest local increase, while its negative gives the direction used by the [[Steepest Descent Method]].

A directional light models illumination whose rays share one direction and whose source is treated as infinitely far away. Unlike a [[Point Light]], it has no meaningful position and does not change direction across the scene.

Sunlight is a common use because the distance to the source is enormous relative to the game world. Surfaces respond according to their orientation toward the light direction.

A discrete grid model replaces continuous space or time with a finite set of sample points. Difference equations relate the value at each point to neighboring values, allowing a computer to approximate differential equations step by step.

Grid spacing controls a central tradeoff. Finer meshes can represent local change more accurately but demand more computation and may require careful numerical treatment to remain stable.

A dish-Sterling plant tracks the Sun with a point-focus mirrored dish and heats a receiver at its focus. A hot-gas Sterling engine converts the receiver heat into shaft work and electrical output, making the arrangement useful for autonomous generation in the source. Hydrogen or helium can be the engine's working fluid. Tracking and optical interception determine the heat reaching the engine.

A displacement gyro indicates an angular position such as pitch, roll, or heading, while a rate gyro indicates angular change per unit time. A restricted single-gimbal rate gyro can support turn indication, whereas freer gyros provide stable attitude or directional references. Pneumatic or electric power keeps the rotor spinning, but each installation introduces characteristic limits and errors.

A distance matrix records the pairwise distance between every pair of observations. It is symmetric when the distance is symmetric, has zeros on its diagonal, and provides the input for many clustering and multidimensional-scaling procedures.

The source constructs one from high-dimensional gene-expression samples. The matrix preserves pairwise relationships without retaining the original feature coordinates, so its meaning depends entirely on the selected distance and preprocessing.

A distance-based outlier has at most a specified proportion or count of observations within a chosen radius. It can be isolated from most of the data by a neighborhood under the selected metric.

The method requires distance and frequency thresholds and does not inherently rank anomalies. It can perform poorly when different regions of the data have different densities.

A distinguishing sequence pattern occurs differently across classes or target groups and is selected for its discriminative signal. Its usefulness depends on contrast, not only high overall support.

Class-aware criteria can expose rare but diagnostic orderings that ordinary frequent-pattern mining would miss. Statistical reliability and redundancy control remain necessary when many candidates are evaluated.

A distributable Blender add-on packages its main initialization file and dependent modules into a predictable directory, commonly delivered as a compressed archive that Blender can install. Metadata describes the package, and registration functions provide the entry points Blender invokes when users enable or disable it.

Distribution should not require recipients to edit development imports or remove diagnostic code. The source's early workflow performs those conversions manually, then its advanced workflow argues for developing directly in the add-on filesystem so the tested structure is already the deployed structure. Packaging is safest when development and installation exercise the same code paths.

A distributed cache is a network-accessible cache shared by several application instances. It gives horizontally scaled processes a common fast copy of data instead of leaving each process with an unrelated in-memory view.

The shared store improves consistency of cached access across instances but adds a remote dependency. Serialization, key design, expiration, invalidation, cache availability, and the behavior on cache failure remain application concerns.

A distributed IT function embeds technology capability in business units rather than concentrating every operational decision in one central department. Local teams can select and use cloud services close to the needs they support.

A shared leadership role still defines standards, governance, and audit expectations, while finance and procurement can manage billing and contracts. Distribution improves responsiveness only when the organization preserves common security, integration, and service-management practices.

A distributed object system lets software objects communicate across process or host boundaries through an interface that resembles local interaction. In AR, tracking, simulation, rendering, and device services may run on different computers while participating in one application.

Distribution can place work near specialized hardware and share state among users. Network delay, partial failure, serialization, and object identity remain real concerns even when the programming abstraction hides connection details.

A distributed scene graph shares a spatial object hierarchy across multiple processes or computers. Participants can render individual viewpoints or operate separate devices while referring to consistent object identities and transformations.

Updates must be communicated and ordered without assuming zero network delay. The design may replicate selected graph state near each renderer while defining which component owns authoritative changes.

A distributed system divides work among independently executing processes that communicate across boundaries rather than sharing one in-process state. This can support independent scaling and deployment, but failures and timing become partial: one component may succeed while another is unavailable.

The book's sales-order system separates message production, queued transport, order persistence, and confirmation. Its design gains resilience to traffic spikes while accepting more complex data integrity, logging, maintenance, and user-experience decisions.

The order-processing discussion contrasts this with a single database transaction that can update an order and stock together. Distributed designs need asynchronous coordination and explicit recovery or compensation rather than assuming every component changes atomically.

Many presenters who decide to use images in their presentation simply go to Google
Image Search, punch in a keyword, and grab the first image they find. This has numer-
ous problems. First and most importantly, the image you find may not add anything but
decoration to the presentation. Images should not just be thematic; they should support
the presentation’s thesis or subtheses in some way, and if they don’t, they can just be
distracting. For example, if you are pitching a new fighting game, a picture of Street
Fighter V may be relevant, but unless you are showing how a particular competing fea-
ture is presented, the audience will be thinking about Street Fighter V instead of what
you are trying to present.
Secondly, presenters often try to stretch low-resolution images to fit the size of the
screen, which makes them pixelated and blurry. Or the presenter tries to cram many
small, low-resolution images onto one slide. Both techniques make for poor legibility.
The rule of thumb is that text and images should be easily legible by the audience
member in the farthest back row of the presentation room.
Finally, in most cases, a copyright holder owns the images you find online, so you do
not necessarily have the license to use them in your presentations.
You can acquire high-resolution, freely usable images through stock image sites, such
as freeimages.com (formerly sxc.hu), and free vector-based art at thenounproject.com,
but be careful that the images you choose do not distract from your points.

A diverging color palette uses two contrasting ordered ramps extending from a light neutral center. It suits values whose sign or direction around a meaningful reference, often zero, matters. For an asymmetric distribution, the class interval containing the reference should align with the neutral color; otherwise the visual center misstates the analytical center. The palette should not be used merely because a variable has a wide range.

A diversion redirects a flight from its original destination to a temporary alternative. The route that later returns from that alternative to the original plan is the recovery leg. A sound diversion recalculates altitude, course, time, fuel, weather, and communication before committing to the new path.

A diversion track must be checked against landmarks and elapsed time after the new heading is established. Before halfway, the [[Double-Error Drift Correction]] can return the aircraft to track in the same elapsed time; after halfway, the [[Opening-Closing Angle Drift Correction]] aims directly toward the destination. If the destination bearing is known reliably, direct tracking can replace both approximations.

A divided difference is a recursively defined coefficient based on function values at distinct nodes. The first divided difference is $f[x_i,x_{i+1}]=(f(x_{i+1})-f(x_i))/(x_{i+1}-x_i)$.

Higher orders compare lower-order divided differences over wider node intervals. A divided-difference table supplies the coefficients for [[Newton Divided Difference Interpolation]].

A Docker container is an isolated running instance created from an image that packages an application and its dependencies. It avoids relying on a target machine to reproduce the exact library and framework environment used during development and testing.

The book runs its .NET Core 3 worker in a Linux container. The container is lighter than copying an entire virtual machine because it packages the application environment while remaining abstracted from much of the host operating system.

A Docker image is the packaged, versionable template used to start one or more containers. It contains the application layers and dependencies described by its Dockerfile but does not become a running process until a container is created from it.

The sales-order image is built locally, tested with `docker run`, tagged, and uploaded to a registry. Kubernetes then refers to that registered image when creating its worker pods.

A Dockerfile is the declarative build recipe for a Docker image. Its instructions choose base images, copy and build application content, establish the runtime entry point, and can use multiple stages to keep the final artifact focused.

Visual Studio generates the book's initial Dockerfile when Linux container support is added. The file remains the reproducible source for rebuilding the image rather than relying on the state of one developer machine.

A document database stores records as self-describing documents rather than rows constrained to one relational table shape. Documents can contain the fields needed for an application object and are commonly addressed through a collection and a unique identifier.

The book presents Cosmos DB as the successor branding for Microsoft's DocumentDB service and accesses work-item documents through a MongoDB-compatible API. Document flexibility does not remove the need for deliberate identifiers, query patterns, and capacity planning.

A dodged bar chart places subgroup bars side by side on a common baseline. This arrangement makes comparisons between subgroup magnitudes easier than stacked segments, though it can become crowded with many categories.

Consistent ordering and a readable legend are essential for tracing each subgroup across the chart.

A domain entity represents a unique object whose identity persists while its attributes and state change. Two entities with identical current property values can still be different because they have different [[Entity Identity]] values. The entity exposes behavior in the [[Ubiquitous Language]] and protects transitions with [[Entity Invariant]]s. This meaning is distinct from a generic database row or a named entity extracted from language: its defining concern is continuity of identity through a life cycle.

A domain event is a fact that changed the state of the domain. It describes something that happened, not something an actor wanted to do, so EventStorming names it with a subject and a past-tense verb such as “Order Confirmed.” Events are placed on an [[Event Timeline]] to reveal causal and temporal relationships. In implementation, the same fact can become an object raised by a [[Domain Entity]] or [[Aggregate]] and later stored through [[Event Sourcing]].

A domain model is a representation in the [[Solution Space]] that expresses domain concepts, state, and behavior in a form software can enforce. It should use the [[Ubiquitous Language]] and make rules discoverable in the model rather than scattering them through controllers or database procedures. A model is selective: it includes what is needed to solve the chosen problem, not every fact about the real world. Unlike an [[Anemic Domain Model]], it incorporates the operations that change its state.

A domain object factory is a named function or method that creates a valid [[Value Object]] or [[Domain Entity]]. It can validate input, convert an external representation, and choose a construction path while keeping an invalid intermediate object from escaping. Multiple factories can make different sources explicit, such as constructing a title from plain text or from sanitized HTML. The factory belongs with the domain type when the creation rules are part of the type's meaning.

A domain service expresses domain behavior that does not naturally belong to one entity or value object. Its interface is defined inside the domain model using the [[Ubiquitous Language]], while an implementation that calls a database or remote system can remain in the [[Application Layer]]. This direction keeps the model free of infrastructure dependencies. Domain services should not become a place to move all behavior out of entities; they are for genuine domain operations whose responsibility spans or sits outside individual objects.
